_README: The Tier 1 blocking core. One recorded decision per term in profanity_wordlists.json: `tier1: true` means Tier 1 may reject a message containing it BEFORE it is sent; `tier1: false` means the term is Tier 2's only, judged by the LLM with the message in front of it. The default for a new or unclassified term is Tier 2 - a term reaches Tier 1 only by carrying a reason here, and tests/test_moderation_tier1_terms.py refuses to load a wordlist term that has no entry at all. The plain-word terms outside English were reviewed by three model families in September 2026 and promoted on a 2-of-3 vote; that is the whole of their provenance, and NO NATIVE SPEAKER HAS REVIEWED ANY LANGUAGE.

_policy.promotion_rule: Evidence-POSITIVE. A term reaches Tier 1 only with a `review` record whose basis is one of: `not_a_word_or_an_identifier` (the needle contains a digit, AND no de-leeting of it spells a word with a recorded ordinary reading - see `a_digit_is_not_evidence_on_its_own`), `curator_attested` (English, checked by a native English speaker for an ordinary English sense), `model_review` (the September 2026 three-family model review - see `_README`; the vote itself is not kept per term), or `native_review` (a named native speaker and date - there are none yet; one supersedes a model review). Absence of a collision is NOT evidence: three rounds of adversarial review found `faggot` (a British dish), `hoer` (one who hoes), Greek `kariola` (a bed), Turkish `kaltak` (a saddle frame), Portuguese `viado` (striped fabric), Korean `byeongsin` (the year 丙申) and `Chuj` (a Mayan language) among terms that scored zero everywhere the gate could look. Adding a language to Tier 1 is a review task, not a code change.
_policy.decision_rule: A term is universal when no supported language has a benign homograph of the surface form Tier 1 matches. `collisions` records every language where wordfreq measures the form at or above the threshold for that language's list size; each one must then carry an `adjudication` of no_benign_sense, or the term stays Tier 2.
_policy.frequency_is_a_tripwire_not_a_decider: wordfreq measures how often a form is written, not whether it is benign. `fuck` scores 4.85 in Danish and 4.29 in German because the swear is borrowed, not because it is innocent there, so automatic demotion on a high score would strip the most universal terms out of Tier 1. The gate is one-directional: a high score forces a recorded adjudication; a low score approves nothing. Absence of a score proves nothing either - zipf_frequency('pica', 'sk') is 0.0 for the one collision the instructions doc had already named.
_policy.length_floor: 4 characters for Latin-script needles, 3 for other alphabets and abugidas, 2 for Hangul, kana and ideographs. Below that, a needle is an ordinary word somewhere among thirty languages and exact matching does not save it.
_policy.matching: Casefold, drop invisible characters, NFC, collapse runs of three or more identical characters. Whole-token equality; no diacritic stripping, no leetspeak or homoglyph folding, no prefix matching, and no language identification of any kind.
_policy.review_status: The wordlist and these decisions were LLM-generated and curated by one non-native curator. NO NATIVE SPEAKER HAS REVIEWED ANY LANGUAGE. The plain-word terms outside English that are in Tier 1 are there on `model_review`: three model families voted, and that is weaker evidence than a native speaker. The frequency gate sees only what a frequency list can see: it is blind to register, regional sense, reclaimed usage, and to every language wordfreq does not carry. Treat `no_collision_measured` as 'nothing objected', not as 'verified safe'.
_policy.what_demotes_a_term: ANY recorded benign reading of the surface form Tier 1 matches demotes the term, whatever kind of word it is: an ordinary common noun (`faggot`, a British dish; `pica`, a typographic unit), a proper noun (`Fucking`, an Austrian village until 2021), or a case-sensitive technical identifier that casefolding merges with the term (`fucK`, the gene symbol for L-fuculokinase, NCBI gene 946022). An earlier revision exempted the last two and recorded them on the term as accepted pre-send false positives instead. That contradicted the decision rule in this same file and it was a gate softening: `The fucK gene encodes L-fuculokinase.` and `The Austrian village of Fucking was renamed Fugging in 2021.` both returned M_FORBIDDEN. The exemption is gone, the key that carried it is gone, and tests/test_moderation_tier1_terms.py fails on any entry that reintroduces either. Tier 1 is smaller for it, which is the trade D1 already makes: a demoted term is judged by Tier 2 with the message in front of it.
_policy.a_digit_is_not_evidence_on_its_own: The digit basis used to read: 'the needle contains a digit, so it can only match a deliberately obfuscated spelling.' The first half is true and the second does not follow. ALPHANUMERIC IDENTIFIERS - gamertags, room and apartment codes, SKUs, model numbers, usernames - substitute a digit for a letter as a matter of course and are ordinary chat content: check_text('Room P1CA is down the hall') and check_text('Model P1CA-200 ships Friday') were both M_FORBIDDEN. What the digit really does is narrow the question from 'is this a word in one of thirty languages?', which nobody here can answer, to 'does an ordinary identifier get spelled this way?', which the recorded readings can. A leet form inherits the readings of the word it spells: `P1CA` reads as a stylized `Pica`. `4RSCHLOCH` was the counter-example that spelled nothing but the slur, until `arschloch` itself was demoted for the German card game of that name - and the re-derivation carried the reading into the leet form and demoted it too, which is the rule working rather than an exception to it. So a needle with a de-leeting in `skeletons_with_a_benign_reading`, or one matching a term this file demotes for a recorded benign reading, is Tier 2's; six terms left Tier 1 on this re-derivation and carry reason `identifier_reading`. The matcher already knew half of it and stopped short: rejoining across punctuation was removed because `p3.der` (a DER certificate), `/api/v1/ado` and `p1.ca` blocked - 198 forms - which fixed the rejoining path and left the compact one, where the same strings without the dot still blocked.

_policy.vocabulary_sweep: wordfreq's 30,000 most frequent words in each of the thirty supported languages are run, as a test, through the Tier 1 matcher. A promoted term may block a word from that list only when the word is the term in its own language, or a collision adjudicated no_benign_sense. Any other hit demotes the term, whatever the vote, with the colliding word recorded under `sweep_collision`; the word is never exempted. The sweep reads one token at a time, so it cannot see a term sitting as a whole token inside an ordinary compound - `marie-salope` - and that class is found by review, not by the sweep.
_policy.spelled_out_forms: A term written with its letters spaced or dotted apart and no digit (`k u r w a`, `đ.ị.t mẹ`, `चू ति या`) is a spelled-out run. Tier 1 rejoins such a run only when it carries a digit, and never across the syllables of an abugida or Hangul, so a spelled-out form is never promoted whatever a review says; it carries reason `spelled_out`, and the compact spelling is a separate term that carries the block.
